name: rachel-s2
description: Rachel, Session 2 (See What Kept Showing Up). Mid-career product manager with three distinct roles + a long-running urban gardening community involvement. Tests the full S2 path: role-by-role exploration, push-for-specific-moments, beyond-the-roles non-work life surfacing, cross-domain pattern naming, principle-naming opener (per PR #132), refinement-pause (per PR #129), and threshold close. The cross-domain pattern Rachel doesn't quite see herself: she keeps building the rituals and rhythms that let groups of people work together durably — at work she calls it 'process design,' in the garden community she just does it. The audit lane PR (S2 scripts-to-principles) will be graded against this golden's candidate run: the conversion should produce more varied, less template-y questions during role exploration, less canned 'I'm noticing something...' pattern naming, and more anchored use of Rachel's own labels for her career and her garden community. Synthetic but representative; replace with PII-scrubbed real session when one is available.
userTurns: My first role was at a small startup, like 12 people, doing project coordination. I'd just graduated with a sociology degree and they needed someone to make their chaos legible. I made the first roadmap. The first sprint board. The first meeting structure that wasn't just 'let's all yell at once.' I wasn't a PM yet — that title came two years later — but I was doing the work.

What I loved was watching engineers stop hating planning. They came in expecting another corporate process and instead I'd ask 'what does your week actually look like, and where does the work fall through the cracks?' We'd build the system from that. They started showing up to standups. Started writing tickets. Not because I forced them, because the system finally fit how they actually worked. Our VP of engineering told me once 'you don't manage people, you build the rooms they want to walk into.' I didn't know what to do with that at the time.

There's one I think about. A senior engineer, Kenji, hadn't merged a PR in three weeks. Everyone thought he was checked out. I asked him what he was working on and he showed me — this enormous refactor he'd been carrying alone because he didn't want to slow anyone down. I built him a three-week 'protected scope' on the roadmap with explicit visibility into what he was doing and why. He merged 40 PRs the next month. The team stopped seeing him as a problem. He thanked me a year later and said 'you saw what I was actually doing.' That's the one I tell.

Second role was a Series B health tech company. Real PM title this time. Three years. The product was a population health platform for clinics — really complex domain. What I ended up doing wasn't really product management in the standard sense. I was the person clinical staff actually trusted to bring their problems to. The engineers respected my requirements docs because they could see I'd talked to actual nurses. The CEO would forward me his messy ideas and I'd come back with 'here's the version of that that's actually shippable.' I was the connective tissue.

The product itself was good but the thing I remember is the rituals I set up. I started a weekly 'show and tell' where engineers demoed to clinicians directly, no PM in the middle. People said it would never work — clinicians wouldn't show up, engineers would clam up. They were wrong. It became the most attended meeting at the company. Clinicians started bringing nurses they wanted to introduce. Engineers started building things specifically to surprise the clinicians. The whole feedback loop changed. I didn't do anything except create the room. The work happened inside it.

Third role is where I am now. Big company, fintech, infrastructure platform team. Real Silicon Valley product org with all the rituals and frameworks. I came in as a senior PM and got promoted to staff after eighteen months. On paper I'm killing it. In practice... I don't know. The work is good. I run the rituals. I write the strategy docs. I do the stakeholder dances. But none of it feels like the thing I'm actually good at. Everything is already structured. Nobody needs me to make the chaos legible because there is no chaos. I'm just maintaining systems other people built.

Outside of work — there's a community garden in my neighborhood I've been involved with for nine years. Started when I bought my condo. I wasn't even particularly into gardening, my dad died right before I moved and I needed somewhere to put my hands. I just showed up to a Saturday work party and stayed. Now I'm the de facto coordinator. Not the president. Just the one who knows everyone's plots, knows what's broken, knows who's about to quit and needs to be checked on.

What I do there — when I think about it now — is the same thing. Last spring we almost lost our lease, the city was pushing development through. The old guard at the garden wanted to fight it, the new families wanted to negotiate, the renters wanted to give up. Everyone was in different meetings, talking past each other. I set up one Saturday where each group presented to the others — what they actually wanted, what they were scared of. I didn't moderate. I just made the room. By the end people who'd been fighting for months were planning together. We kept the garden.

I never thought of those as the same thing. The work thing and the garden thing. At work I call it 'process design' or 'cross-functional alignment' or whatever the framework du jour is. At the garden I just call it 'showing up.' But you're naming them as one thing.

Yeah. People come to me when groups need to actually work together — not in the corporate sense, in the durable sense. Where the rhythms have to hold even when the people change. Even when the stakes change. Even when the funding goes away.

I think so. Yes — that does land. Continuity Over Uniqueness. The pattern persists. Whether I'm at the startup, the health tech company, the big fintech, or the garden — I'm doing the same thing. Building the rooms people want to walk into. Building the rituals that let groups hold together over time.
No. That's it. We found it.
